situation: You began three new skincare products at the same time a week ago, and your face now stings. Because all three started together, the sting could come from one product, from two of them interacting, or from something unrelated that changed that week. How severe the reaction is, and whether it is fading or getting worse, is unknown and decides how cautious to be.

minds.title: The Experimenter
minds.concern: Isolating the cause through controlled, one-change-at-a-time testing rather than guessing.
minds.author: Claude Bernard
minds.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

minds.title: The Subtractor
minds.concern: Removing possible harms first, because adding more to an irritated situation is the riskier move.
minds.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

minds.title: The Story Skeptic
minds.concern: Guarding against quick, confident causal stories built from a vague feeling and a short memory.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Three new products, one stinging face: that is three suspects and no alibis. Pull them all, let the skin settle, then bring them back one at a time, a week or so apart. Whichever one brings the sting back is your answer.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: I would stop first and investigate later. Starting three products at once was the real gamble. Hidden harm lives in additions, so subtraction comes first: gentle cleanser, plain moisturizer, sunscreen, nothing else. It is cheap, reversible, and rarely makes anything worse. That is the via negativa idea.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Story Skeptic
debate.text: Careful, both of you. The quick-thinking mind loves a villain, and the product with the scariest ingredient list will get blamed. Stinging can also come from weather, a new pillowcase, a hot shower habit. Before convicting anything, list every change from last week, not just the three.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: My method survives that. The bare routine is the baseline. If the sting fades, the cause was in the removed products or their combination. If it does not, your list of other changes becomes the lead. Either outcome teaches you something, which guessing never does.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: I would go further than Taleb here, because combinations matter. Three products might each be fine alone and harsh together, like two exfoliating acids layered. Testing singly could acquit every one of them while the stack is the culprit. If singles come back clean, test pairs.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Story Skeptic
debate.text: That complicates the tidy story, good. Also, sting is a weak signal. Some products tingle briefly on anyone and that is not damage. Decide in advance what counts: lasting redness, burning after rinsing, flaking. Otherwise your memory of last Tuesday becomes the data, and memory is a sloppy lab.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Then write it down. A two-line daily log: what went on, how it felt at ten minutes and at an hour. Notes beat impressions. I would also patch test each product on the inner forearm or behind the ear before it goes back on the face.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: Patch tests are weaker than they look. Facial skin is thinner and reacts differently from a forearm. And waiting has a cost: bring a product back too early on a damaged barrier and you restart the clock. I would wait until the skin has felt normal for several days, longer than you want.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Conceded: a slow trial beats a fast one if the baseline is shaky. But I will not concede skipping reintroduction. Without it you only know that something among three hurt, not which, and you may bin a product that works for you.
debate.author: Claude Bernard
debate.book: An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine
debate.basis: Basis: Claude Bernard, An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine

debate.speaker: The Story Skeptic
debate.text: And nobody has named the exit ramp. Swelling, hives, blistering, spreading rash, or pain that keeps worsening means stop experimenting and get it looked at by a doctor or pharmacist. A home trial assumes mild irritation. The experiment is only safe inside that boundary.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: Agreed, and that settles my worry. I accept an experiment that starts by subtracting and has a tripwire. What we still disagree on is whether every product deserves a retrial, or whether dropping one suspect for good is the wiser, cheaper loss.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

clearer: The main insight is that a stinging face after three simultaneous starts cannot be solved by thinking harder about ingredients; it needs a calm baseline first and then changes made one at a time, with notes instead of impressions. Still disputed is how patient to be (how long to wait before reintroducing) and whether every product deserves a second try or a suspect can simply be dropped. A possible self-reflection: which of the three products do you most want to keep, and how much would you lose by never retesting it?
dependsOn: If the sting is mild and fading once you pause everything except a gentle cleanser, plain moisturizer and sunscreen, then a slow reintroduction becomes reasonable, one product every one to two weeks (longer if skin reacts), because that is the only way to separate a single culprit from a combination. If the sting is not fading, or other things changed last week (weather, a new detergent or pillowcase, a different routine), then those other changes deserve checking before blaming the products. If you see swelling, hives, blistering, a spreading rash, or pain that keeps worsening, a doctor or pharmacist should look at it before any further testing. If one product is not essential to you, dropping it permanently without retesting is a cheaper, legitimate choice. The decisive unknown is whether the reaction is irritation or something more serious; a few days on the bare routine, plus a short note on what you see, is a proportionate way to learn it.
